la:verb:occumbo.html:
occumbo (obc-), cŭbui, cŭbĭtum, 3, v. n.
ob-cumbo, cubo
,
to fall or sink down (cf.: occido, obeo, oppeto); hence,
To go down, to set, of the heavenly bodies (postclass.): cometes cum oriretur occumberetque,: cum sol occumberet,; .—
To fall dying, to die (the class. signif. of the word); constr. absol. or with mortem, morte, or morti.
Absol.: cum veter occubuit Priamus, fell, Enn. ap. P. (Ann. v. 17 Vahl.): aut occubuissem honeste, aut victores hodie viveremus,: pro libertate cos occubuisse, : circa se dimicans occubuerat,: fertur et ante annos occubuisse suos,: dederat ne ferro occumbere posset,: acie,.—
With mortem or morte (the vacillation of MSS. between these two forms makes it difficult to ascertain which was the prevailing one; cf. Zumpt, Gr. § 387; Krebs, Antibarb. p. 790): pro patriā mortem (al. morte) occumbere, (Kühner, Moser, Orelli, and Baiter have mortem, Klotz and Fischer morte): quod liberata patria ... mortem occubuisset,; ; : qui pugnantes mortem occubuissent,. —So, too, letum, Enn. ap. P. (Ann. v. 390 Vahl.): necem voluntariam, (al., with inferior MSS., nece voluntariā): ictus clavā morte occubuit, Weissenb. ad loc.: morte occumbentis,: ambo pro republicā morte occubuisse,.—
With morti (perh. only poet.): pro vostrā vitā morti occumbant obviam. Enn. ap. (Trag. v. 176 Vahl.); so, certae morti, l. l.: neci,.—
To succumb to, fall by the hand of one (poet.).—With dat.: Rullo ditissimus agri Occumbis,; .—With per: per te vidit Vulcani occumbere prolem,. —*
Like accumbere, to lie at table, Afran. ap. .

la:verb:occubo.gloss: to lie or fall in, on, or down, especially in the grave; rest, repose
senses: to lie or fall in, on, or down, especially in the grave; rest, repose
la:verb:occubo.html:
occŭbo, āre, 1, v. n.
ob-cubo
,
to lie in a place; to rest, repose in the grave (poet.): ad tumulum, quo maximus occubat Hector,: Paris urbe paternā occubat,: crudelibus occubat umbris,reposes with the dead,: flebili leto,: consul pro vestrā victoriā morte occubans,.

senses: to seize, invade, take possession of
to anticipate, make the first move
la:verb:occupo.html:
occŭpo, āvi, ātum, 1 (occupassis for occupaveris, :
occupassit for occupaverit,), v. a.
obcapio; lit., to lay hold of; hence
, to take possession of, seize, occupy any thing (esp. a place; class.; cf.: expugno, obsideo).
Lit.: totam Italiam suis praesidiis obsidere atque occupare cogitat,: locum,: possessiones,: urbes,: montem,: portum,: aditum,to go in, enter,: regnum,: tyrannidem,: familiam optimam occupavit,has got hold of, has got into,: occupando adquirere aliquid, sqq.; cf. : vindemia occupabit sementem,shall reach to,.—Poet.: aliquem amplexu,to clasp in one's arms, to embrace,.—
Transf.
To occupy, i. e. to take up, fill with any thing: atrā nube polum,: urbem (sc. aedificiis),: caementis Tyrrhenum mare,.—
To fall upon, attack one with any thing (syn. invado): Latagum saxo ... Occupat os faciemque adversam,: aliquem gladio,: aliquem morsu,: canes ense,, 82 (5, 4, 84): ne occupet te pluvia,: caligo, id. Job, 3, 5.—Poet., in a friendly sense, to surprise: Volteium Philippus Vilia vendentem Occupat,.—
To get the start of, to be beforehand with, to anticipate, to do a thing first, to outstrip: occupat egressas quamlibet ante rates,: volo, tu prior ut occupes adire,that you should present yourself the first,: praeloqui,: bellum facere,to begin the war first,: rapere oscula,.—
Trop.
To seize, take possession of, fill, invade, engross: tantus timor omnem exercitum occupavit,: tremor occupat artus,: sopor occupat artus,: animos magnitudine rei,: pallor ora,.—
To take up, occupy, employ: haec causa primos menses occupabit, Cael. ap. : cum in mentem venit tres et sexaginta annos aeque multa volumina occupasse mihi,: in funambulo Animum,: contio, quae homines occupatos occupat,: tanta superstitio mentis Siculorum occupavit,: pecuniam, to put out or lay out money: pecuniam adulescentulo grandi fenore occupavisti,have loaned it at a high rate,: pecunias apud populos,: pecuniam animalibus,to lay out, invest in cattle,: pecuniam in pecore,: argentum,.—Pass.: ante occupatur animus ab iracundiā,; .—Hence, oc-cŭpātus, a, um, P. a., taken up, occupied, employed, busy, engaged (class.): ut si occupati profuimus aliquid civibus nostris, prosimus etiam otiosi,: in eo, ut,: tempora,: qui in patriā delendā occupati et sunt et fuerunt,: hostibus opere occupatis,: .—Hence, married, occupatae (opp. to vacuae), .—Comp.: comitiorum dilationes occupatiorem me habebant, Cael. ap. .—Sup.: non dubito, quin occupatissimus fueris,very much occupied,; .

Octāvĭus, i, m.; Octāvĭa, ae, f.,
the name of a Roman gens, ; cf. Drumann, History of Rome, vol. iv. p. 218 sq.
C. Octavius, the father of theemperor Augustus, ; .—
Cn. Octavius, the first consul of this gens, .—
M. Octavius Caecina, a tribune of the people, .—
Rarely of the emperor Augustus, .—
In the fem., Octavia, the name of the two sisters of the emperor Augustus, ; ; .—
Octavia was also the name of the daughter of the emperor Claudius and Messalina, ; .—
Octaviae Porticus, two halls in Rome, ; ; ; Paul. ex Müll.—Hence,
Octāvĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to an Octavius, Octavian: Octaviano bello,i. e. in the war of the consul Cn. Octavius with Cinna,: milites,of M. Octavius, who fought for Pompey,.—Esp., subst.: Octāvĭānus, i, m., a surname of the emperor Augustus, who was adopted out of the gens Octavia into the gens Julia, ; ; ; .

senses: luminary of the sun and stars
spot resembling an eye, such as on a peacock feather
bud, bulb or knob on many roots, on the reed, etc.
eye of the soul, mind's eye
la:noun:oculus.html:
ŏcŭlus (sync. oclus, Prud. στεφ. 10, 592 dub.), i, m.
kindr. with Sanscr. akshi and aksha, from the root ītsh, videre; Gr. ὄσσομαι, ὄσσε; Goth. augō; Germ. Auge; Engl. eye
,
an eye.
Lit.: quae (natura) primum oculos membranis tenuissimis vestivit et saepsit ... sed lubricos oculos fecit et mobiles,; cf. ; ; 3, 59, 221: venusti,: eminentes,prominent,: oculi tanquam speculatores,: acuti,: maligni,: minaces,: oculos conicere in aliquem, to cast or fix one's eyes upon, : oculos conjecit in hostem,: adicere alicui rei, to cast one's eyes upon, glance at: ad eorum ne quem oculos adiciat suos,; to covet, : adicere ad rem aliquam,: de aliquo nusquam deicere,to never turn one's eyes away from, to regard with fixed attention,: deicere ab aliquā re,to turn away,: in terram figere,to fix one's eyes upon the ground,: deicere in terram,to cast down to,: demittere,: erigere,: attollere. ; : circumferre,: premere,: deponere, to fix, Hor C. 1, 36, 18: distorquere,: spargere,to direct hither and thither,: oculis cernere,to see with one's own eyes,: oculos auferre spectanti,to blind the eyes of an observer, to cheat him before his eyes,: ponere sibi aliquid ante oculos. i. e. to imagine to one's self any thing, : proponere oculis suis aliquid,: esse ante oculos,to be before one's eyes,: res posita in oculis, and ante oculos, that lies before one's eyes, is apparent, evident: de rebus ante oculos positis,: omnia sunt enim posita ante oculos,: inque meis oculis candida Delos erat,before my eyes,: vivere in oculis, habitare in oculis, to live in the sight of, in the presence of, in intercourse with: in maximā celebritate atque in oculis civium quondam viximus,: habitavi in oculis,; cf.: in foro palam Syracusis in ore atque in oculis provinciae,; ; ; : habere in oculis,to keep in sight, to watch, observe,: in oculis omnium submergi,: se ante oculos suos trucidari sinerent,; ; : ab oculis alicujus abire (ire), to leave one's presence: Abin' hinc ab oculis?; ; ; cf.: ab oculis recedere,: ab oculis concedere,: (angues) conspecti repente ex oculis abierunt,out of sight,: prodigii species ex oculis elapsa,: (avem) ablatam ex oculis,: facesserent propere ex urbe ab ore atque oculis populi Romani,: sub oculis alicujus,before a person's eyes, in his presence,; : sub oculis domini esse,: quos honores sub oculis tuis gessit,: sub avi oculis necari,; : hostes sub oculis erant,; : sub oculis Caesaris,: hunc oculis suis nostrarum numquam quisquam vidit, with his own eyes, i. e. actually, in person, : numquam ante hunc diem meis oculis eam videram,: ad oculum, for display, to be seen: non ad oculum servientes,; .—As a term of endearment, the apple of my eye, my darling: ubi isti sunt quibus vos oculi estis, quibus vitae estis, quibus deliciae?: bene vale, ocule mi! —Hence, in a double sense: par oculorum in amicitiā M. Antonii triumviri,.—The ancients swore by their eyes: si voltis per oculos jurare, nihilo magis facietis,.—
Transf.
The power of seeing, sight, vision: ut eum quoque oculum, quo bene videret, amitteret, lost, i. e. became blind, : oculos perdere,: restituere alicui,; cf.: oculis usurpare rem,i. e. see,.—
A luminary, said of the sun and stars (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): mundi oculus. i. e. the sun, : stellarum oculi,.—
A spot resembling an eye, as on a panther's hide, a peacock's tail, etc., : pavonum caudae,. —So arch. t. t.: oculus volutae,. —
Of plants.
An eye, bud, bourgeon: oculos imponere, i. e. to bud, inoculate, : gemmans,.—
A bulb or knob on many roots, on the reed, etc.: harundinis,; : seritur harundo bulbo radicis, quem alii oculum vocant,.—
A plant, called also aizoum majus, . —
Trop.
A principal ornament: hi duo illos oculos orae maritimae effoderunt (Corinth and Carthage), : ex duobus Graeciae oculis,i. e. Athens and Sparta,.—
The eye of the soul, the mind's eye: eloquentiam quam nullis nisi mentis oculis videre possumus,: acrioribus mentis oculis intueri,: oculos pascere re aliquā,to feast one's eyes on any thing,; cf.: concupiscentia oculorum, Joh. 2, 16: fructum oculis (dat.) capere ex aliquā re, : oculi dolent, the eyes ache, i. e. one is afflicted by something seen, ; Cael. ap. ; cf.: pietas, pater, oculis dolorem prohibet,i. e. forbids me to take offence,: in oculis, in the eye, i. e. in view, hoped or expected: frumenti spes, quae in oculis fuerat, utrosque frustrata pariter,: acies et arma in oculis erant,: Philotae supplicium in oculis erat,: esse in oculis,to be beloved, esteemed,: esse in oculis multitudinis,: ferre, gestare in oculis, to love, esteem, value: oderat tum, cum, etc....jam fert in oculis,: rex te ergo in oculis,: aequis oculis videre, i. e. contentedly, with satisfaction (like aequo animo), : ante oculos, in mind, in view: mors ante oculos debet esse,; ; also plain, obvious: simul est illud ante oculos,: sit ante oculos Nero,i. e. set him before you, consider him,: ante oculos habere, to keep in mind (post-class.): habe ante oculos hanc esse terram,: mortalitatem,; ; for which (late Lat.) prae oculis: prae oculis habere terrorem futuri judicii, Greg. M. Ep. 2, 48; 3, 27 al.: nec jam fas ullum prae oculis habent,: ob oculos versari, to be before the mind, etc.: mors (ei) ob oculos versatur,; ; cf.: usu versatur ante oculos vobis Glaucia,; ; ; ; : ponere aliquid ante oculos, to call up in mind, imagine, etc.: eā (translatione) utimur rei ante oculos ponendae causā,: ora eorum ponite vobis ante oculos,: calamitatem Cottae sibi ante oculos ponunt,: exsilium Cn. Marci sibi proponunt ante oculos,: conjurationem ante oculos ponere,: studia eorum vobis ante oculos proponere,; rarely: constituere sibi aliquid ante oculos,; : ante oculos ponere (proponere), with ellips. of dat. of person, ; ; ; ; : nec a re publicā deiciebam oculos,.

senses: to be lost, undone or ruined
la:verb:occido.html:
occĭdo, cĭdi, cāsum, 3, v. n.
obcado
,
to fall down, fall.
Lit.
In gen. (rare): et alia Signa de caelo ad terram occidunt,: ut alii

super alios occiderent, : arbores ita inciderant, ut momento levi impulsae occiderent,.—

In partic.
Of the heavenly bodies, to go down, set (class.): prope jam occidente sole, Pac. ap. : soles occidere, et redire possunt: Nobis, cum semel occidit brevis lux, Nox est perpetua una dormienda,: Capra, Aquila, Canicula,: occasura pars caeli,i. e. western,: SOL OCCASVS SVPREMA TEMPESTAS ESTO, i. e. sundown, sunset, Lex XII. Tab.; cf. ( Müll., gives, instead of it, OCCASVS SOLIS; v. 2. occasus); so, ante solem obcasum,before sunset,: donec lux occidat,.—Fig.: non occidet ultra sol tuus,.—
Pregn., to fall, perish, die (class.; syn.: obeo, pereo, intereo): exstincto calore, occidimus ipsi et extinguimur,: in bello,: Eudemus proelians ad Syracusas occidit,: sperans hostium saevitiā facile eum occasurum,: occiderit ferro Priamus?: dextrā suā, to die by one's own hand (by suicide), : minimo vulnere,.—
Transf., to perish, be ruined, lost, etc.
Of persons: sin plane occidimus,.—So, esp., occidi, an exclamation of despair, I am lost, undone, ; : nulla sum, nulla sum: tota tota occidi,: occidimus funditus,.—
Of things: non hercle occiderunt mihi etiam fundique atque aedes,I have not yet lost,: occidit spes nostra,is gone,: lumen (oculorum),: dolus,: causa,: rem publicam occidere,: vita,: occidit ornatus (mundi),perishes,: vestra beneficia occasura esse,.—Hence, occĭdens, entis, P. a.; as subst., m., the quarter of the setting sun, the west, the occident (class.): ab oriente ad occidentem,: vel occidentis usque ad ultimum sinum,: cui se oriens occidensque submiserat,: validissima in se civium arma viribus occidentis coepta,: partes mundi, Paul. ex Müll.

la:noun:occupatio.html:
occŭpātĭo, ōnis, f.
occupo
,
a taking possession of a thing; a seizing, occupying (class.).
Lit. (very rare): fori,: vetus,a taking possession, seizure,.—
Transf.
Rhet. t. t.: ante occupatio, an anticipation of an opponent's objections, (but in , the true reading is occultatio, q. v.).—
A business, employment, occupation (the usual meaning, esp. of public service; cf. studium): in maximis occupationibus tuis numquam intermittis studia doctrinae,: maximis occupationibus distinebar,: nullis occupationibus inplicatus,: ille aut occupatione aut difficultate tardior tibi erit visus,: ab omni occupatione se expedire,: relaxare se occupatione,.—With gen.: neque has tantularum rerum occupationes sibi Britanniae anteponendas judicabat,engaging in such trivial affairs,.

la:verb:occurro.gloss: to run into; to go to meet
senses: to run into; to go to meet
to meet, go to, come to
to answer, reply, especially in objection
to present oneself, suggest oneself, appear, occur, especially to the mind
la:verb:occurro.html:
oc-curro (obc-), curri, rarely cucurri (; ), cursum, 3 (archaic
perf. occecurri, like memordi, peposci, Aelius Tubero ap. ), v. n., to run up to, run to meet; to go or come up to, to go or come to meet, to meet (class.; syn. obvenio).
Lit.
In gen.: ilico Occucurri atque interpello,: Caesari venienti,: obviam alicui,to go to meet,: amicis,; .—Impers.: occurritur (sc. mihi),.—
In partic., to go against, rush upon, attack an enemy: duabus Fabianis legionibus occurrit,: armatis,: telis occurrere,: obvius adversoque occurrit,.—
Transf.
To come to, meet, fall in with any thing: quibuscumque signis occurrerat, se aggregabat,: tot vatibus,.—
To go or come to any place.
With dat.: concilio,. —
With ad: legati ad id concilium occurrerunt,.—
With in and acc.: in aliam civitatem occurrere,.—
Of situation.
To stand or lie opposite to: apud Elegiam occurrit ei (Euphrati) Taurus mons,.—
To lie in the way of, meet as an obstacle: in asperis locis silex saepe impenetrabilis ferro occurrebat,.—
Trop.
To obviate or seek to obviate, to meet, resist, oppose, counteract: omnibus ejus consiliis occurri atque obstiti,: illi rationi,: malevolentiae hominum, Brut. ap. .—
To cure or attempt to cure; to relieve, remedy: venienti occurrite morbo,: exspectationi,: rei sapientiā occurrere,; .—
To meet with words, i. e. to answer, reply, object: ut si dicenti, Quem video? ita occurras, ego,: Venus,.—Impers. pass.: occurretur enim, sicut occursum est,: occurritur autem nobis, et quidem a doctis et

eruditis, etc., .—

To offer or present itself, suggest itself, appear, occur: tu occurrebas dignus eo munere,: nec tamen mihi quicquam occurrit cur, etc.,; : Atheniensium classis demersae et exercitus deleti occurrebant,; cf.: ea cum universa occurrerent animo,: oculis ejus tot paludes occurrerent,: oras ad Eurum sequentibus nihil memorabile occurrit,: animo,presents itself to his mind, occurs to him,; cf.: ea quae occurrant,: una defensio occurrit, quod muneribus tuis obniti non debui,: cogitationi, quonam modo, etc.,: neque vos paeon, aut herous ille conturbet: ipsi occurrent orationi,will present themselves,: haec tenenda sunt oratori: saepe enim occurrunt,often occur,: quodcumque in mentem veniat, aut quodcumque occurrat,: ne quid honestum occurreret,.— With inf.: occurrit et aliqua dicere de magicis (herbis),it seems proper,.—
To reach, attain (eccl. Lat.): donec occurramus in unitatem fidei,: si quo modo occurram ad resurrectionem,.

la:noun:occasio.html:
occāsĭo, ōnis, f.
occĭdo, a falling out, a happening, hap; hence
,
an occasion, opportunity, fit time, convenient season, favorable moment for doing any thing; εὐκαιρία, καιρός (syn.: opportunitas, locus, facultas).
In gen.: occasio est pars temporis, habens in se alicujus rei idoneam faciendi aut non faciendi opportunitatem ... in occasione, ad spatium temporis, faciendi quaedam opportunitas intellegitur adjuncta,: tempus actionis opportunum Graece εὐκαιρία, Latine appellatur occasio, : occasio opportunitas temporis casu quodam provenientis est, Paul. ex Müll.: dum datur mihi occasio Tempusque,; cf.: nunc occasio est et tempus,; : an ego occasionem tantam, tam brevem, tam optatam, tam insperatam Amitterem?: minima,; cf. summa, infra: occasionem nancisci, Afran. ap. : quem, si interficere voluisset, quantae quoties occasiones, quam praeclarae fuerunt,: occasio opprimendi,: inrumpendi in urbem,: resistendi,: majores occasiones ad opitulandum haberem, more opportunities, Planc

up. : ut primum occasio data est rem publicam defendendi,as soon as an opportunity presented itself,: occasionem sibi ad occupandam Asiam oblatam esse arbitratur,has presented itself,: amplam occasionem calumniae nactus,: occasio mirifica,: opportuna,: quo faciliorem occasionem Salvio praebuit perficiendi conata,: occasio minor opinione,: tam bona,: lepida,: bellissima,: occasionem amittere,to lose, let slip,: omittere,; so, praetermittere,: capere,to seize,: arripere,: occasiones quaerere,: rapere de die,: amplecti,: sumere,: occasione uti,: non deesse occasioni,not to miss, to profit by,: cunctationem hostium suam fore occasionem rati,: dum datur mihi occasio tempusque,: ne a fortunā datam occasionem liberandae Graeciae dimitterent,; : cujus (rei) se occasio dederit,: (paratus) depugnare, si occasio tulerit, mori, si casus inciderit, etc., Planc. ap. : occasionem aperire ad invadendum,: occasionem sibi ad occupandam Asiam oblatam esse,: occasione datā,should an opportunity offer,; cf.: occasione oblatā simultates deponere,: praebere,: offerre,: per occasionem,on a favorable opportunity,: rem inmaturam nisi per occasionem aperire noluerat,; ; ; : fratris memoriā per omnem occasionem celebratā,on every occasion,; : ad occasionem aurae evehi,the wind being fair, taking advantage of a fair wind,: levia proelia ex occasione hujus aut illius partis oriebantur,: ex occasione,as occasion offered,: occasione omni,on every occasion,.—With inf.: nunc adest occasio Benefacta cumulare = occasio cumulandi,: nunc est illa occasio inimicum ulcisci,: agere tuam rem occasio est,; ; ; cf.: summa eludendi occasio'st mihi nunc senes Et Phaedriae curam adimere,.—With ut and subj.: fuit occasio, si vellet, jam pridem argentum ut daret,: quoniam occasio fuit Mea virtute parta ut quantum velles sumeres,: rara haec occasio est, ut referri possint divini honores,.—

Personified: Occasio, Opportunity, as a goddess, ; .—
In partic.
Opportunity.
Facility or means of having a thing: solitudinis,.—
A supply, stock (post-Aug.): oleae,: lapidum,: vetusti olei,.—
A pretext, plea, plausible explanation: hāc illi opus est occasione, ne illum talium precum pudeat,: occasiones et ex causis et ex dictis adversariorum oriuntur,; : quantulacunque adeo est occasio, sufficit irae,.—

ōcĭor, ōcĭus (

Lit.: et ventis, et fulminis ocior alis,; : ocior cervis, Ocior Euro,; : aurā,; 2, 20, 13: fugit ocior aurā,: verbere,: Tigris ocior remeat,: ociore ambitu,: ociore spatio,.—
Transf., of time, quicker, sooner, earlier; sup.: ficorum ocissima senectus,: pira,the soonest ripe,: venenum,.—Hence, adv.: ōcĭ-ter; comp. ōcĭus; sup. ocissĭme (old collat. form oxime, Paul. ex Müll.); quickly, swiftly, speedily (class. only in the comp. and sup.; cf.: ocius secundae collationis et deinde tertiae ocissime frequentata sunt, etc., Paul. ex Müll.).
Posit. (ante- and post-class.): ociter serva cives, Enn. ap. , acc. to Vahl. ad : profer ociter,; p. 125, 8.—
Comp., more quickly or speedily, sooner, etc.: idque ocius faciet, si, etc.,: ut ocius ad tuum pervenias,: recreantur ocius,: omnium Versatur urna, serius ocius Sors exitura, sooner or later, : angulus iste feret piper et tus ocius uvā,sooner than, rather than,: ocius illud extorquebis,i. e. more easily,.—
Sometimes the comp. is used in gen. for quickly, speedily: sequere hac me ocius, Ter Heaut. 4, 7, 4: gladio occursat,: nemon' oleum fert ocius?quickly,; ; : heus Phaedrome, exi, exi, exi, inquam, ocius,.—
Sup., very quickly or speedily: ocissime nos liberi possumus fieri, Plaut. Fragm. ap. Paul. ex Müll.: quam ocissume ad provinciam accedat,as speedily as possible,: ferre,: sanant ulcera,.

la:noun:oceanus.html:
Ōcĕănus, i, m. (rarely Ōcĕănum, i, n.), = Ὠκεανός,
the great sea that encompasses the land, the ocean: omnis terra parva quaedam insula est, circumfusa illo mari, quod Atlanticum, quod magnum, quem Oceanum appellatis in terris,: Oceanum rubra obruit aethra, Enn. ap. (Ann. p. 418 Vahl.): Oceani ostium,; cf. : Oceani freta,i. e. the Strait of Gades, Strait of Gibraltar,; cf. : quae sunt maritimae civitates Oceanumque attingunt,: circumvagus,circumfluent,; cf. circumfusus,: dissociabilis,: beluosus,: ruber,.—The form Oceanum, n., is found only in apposition with mare: quam (insulam) mare Oceanum circumluit,.—In acc.: proximus mare Oceanum,; cf.: se in nostrum et Oceanum mare extendit,.—In dat.: mari Oceano,.—In abl.: mari Oceano aut amnibus longinquis saeptum imperium,.—(Supposed examples of the adjectival use of Oceanus, as Oceano fluctu and litore, in and 113 Jan; Oceanas aquas, Ven. Carm. 3, 9, 4; Oceanis aquis,, are dub.; several edd. read in Juv., Oceani; and in Ven., in the first passage, Oceanus, and in the second, Oceani.)—
Personified, as a deity, the son of Cœlus and Terra, the husband of Tethys, and the father of the rivers and nymphs, ; ; Hyg. Fab. praef.; .—The ancient philosophers regard water as the primary element of all things; hence: Oceanumque patrem rerum,.—
Transf.
A large bathing-tub (postclass.), .—
A Roman surname, ; ; ; .—
Hence, †
ōcĕănensis, e, adj., of or belonging to the ocean, situated by the sea-side, Eckhel. D. N. 8, p. 110.—
ōcĕănītis, ĭdis, f., a daughter of Ocean: Clioque et Beroe soror, Oceanitides ambae,; Hyg. Fab. praef.

la:verb:occulo.html:
occŭlo (obc-), cŭlŭi, cultum, 3 (
plup. sync. occulerat, ), v. a.
obcolo
, to cover, cover over (syn.: tego, condo, celo, abdo).
In gen. (very rare): terra occulit caput, Enn. ap. Paul. ex Müll. (Trag. v. 141 Vahl.): virgulta multā terrā,.—
In partic., to cover up, hide, conceal (class.; esp. in the P. a.;v.in the foll.): vitia corporis fuco,: vulnera,: (feminae) parietum umbris occuluntur,are kept concealed,: hastatos,: se silvā,: classem in convexo nemorum sub rupe,: caligine terras,: puncta argumentorum,: narratum ab iis,to keep secret, conceal,: vitia,.— Absol.: si quis et imprudens aspexerit, occulat ille,.—*
Of burying: occultum efferre significat sub terram ferre, ponere, Paul. ex Müll.—Hence, occultus (archaic orthogr. OQVOLTVS, S. C. Bacch.; scanned ŏccultus,; ; ; cf. Brix, Trin. Einleit. p. 14 Ritschl ad l. l. ed. 2), a, um, P. a., hidden, concealed, secret (freq. and class.; syn. abditus): hi saltem in occultis locis prostant, vos in foro ipso,: res occultae et penitus abditae,: occultiores insidiae,: occultior atque tectior cupiditas,: si quid erit occultius et reconditum,: cum res occultissimas aperueris in lucemque protuleris,: per occultos calles,: via,: nota,: sapor,: crescit, occulto velut arbor aevo, Fama Marcelli,from an obscure, remote age,: res,i. e. the hidden laws of nature,; ; ; ; ; : occulti miranda potentia fati,.—
Of persons, close, reserved, secret, not open: si me astutum et occultum lubet fingere,: ab occultis cavendum hominibus consultisque,; .—With gen.: occultus odii,dissembling his hate,.—
Occultus, adverbially for occulte, in secret, secretly (Tacitean): qui ejusmodi preces occulti illuderent,; : patris mei amicitias non occulti ferunt,.—
Neutr. as subst.
oc-culta, ōrum, plur., secret things or places, secrets: servi, quibus occulta creduntur,: cui fervens Aestuat occultis animus semperque tacendis,. —With gen.: occulta saltuum scrutari,: occulta conjurationis retexere,: occulta cordis,: hominum,: ab occultis meis,from my secret sins,.—
Sing.: occultum, i, n., secrecy, only in adverb. phrases, in occulto; per occultum; ex occulto, in secret, secretly: SACRA IN OQVOLTOD NE QVIQVAM FECISE VELET, S. C. Bacch.: in occulto mussabant, ap. Paul. ex Müll. (Ann. v. 185 Vahl.): : stare in occulto,: per occultum (post-Aug.), Tac.

A. 6, 7; 4, 71 fin.; 5, 4; : ex occulto,from a place of concealment, secret place,: Jugurtha ex occulto repente nostros invadit,.—Hence, secretly: ex occulto intervenire,.—Hence, adv., in three forms: occultē (class.), occultō (ante-class.), and occultim (post-class.), in concealment, in secret, secretly, privately.

Form occulte: neque id occulte fert,does not keep it secret, makes no secret of it, does not conceal it,: ea nunc occulte cuniculis oppugnatur,: proficisci,: inter se constituere aliquid,: labitur occulte,: nec clam illud occulteque factum est,.—
Form occulto, Afran. ap. P. (Com. Rel. v. 295 Rib.).— *
Form occultim: reptare,.—
Comp.: conari occultius,: erant praeterea complures paulo occultius consilii hujus participes,: .—Sup.: quam potuit occultissime reliquas cohortes duxit,: castra quam potest occultissime locat,; ; for which maxime occulte,.

la:verb:occurro#2.html:
oc-curro (obc-), curri, rarely cucurri (; ), cursum, 3 (archaic
perf. occecurri, like memordi, peposci, Aelius Tubero ap. ), v. n., to run up to, run to meet; to go or come up to, to go or come to meet, to meet (class.; syn. obvenio).
Lit.
In gen.: ilico Occucurri atque interpello,: Caesari venienti,: obviam alicui,to go to meet,: amicis,; .—Impers.: occurritur (sc. mihi),.—
In partic., to go against, rush upon, attack an enemy: duabus Fabianis legionibus occurrit,: armatis,: telis occurrere,: obvius adversoque occurrit,.—
Transf.
To come to, meet, fall in with any thing: quibuscumque signis occurrerat, se aggregabat,: tot vatibus,.—
To go or come to any place.
With dat.: concilio,. —
With ad: legati ad id concilium occurrerunt,.—
With in and acc.: in aliam civitatem occurrere,.—
Of situation.
To stand or lie opposite to: apud Elegiam occurrit ei (Euphrati) Taurus mons,.—
To lie in the way of, meet as an obstacle: in asperis locis silex saepe impenetrabilis ferro occurrebat,.—
Trop.
To obviate or seek to obviate, to meet, resist, oppose, counteract: omnibus ejus consiliis occurri atque obstiti,: illi rationi,: malevolentiae hominum, Brut. ap. .—
To cure or attempt to cure; to relieve, remedy: venienti occurrite morbo,: exspectationi,: rei sapientiā occurrere,; .—
To meet with words, i. e. to answer, reply, object: ut si dicenti, Quem video? ita occurras, ego,: Venus,.—Impers. pass.: occurretur enim, sicut occursum est,: occurritur autem nobis, et quidem a doctis et

eruditis, etc., .—

To offer or present itself, suggest itself, appear, occur: tu occurrebas dignus eo munere,: nec tamen mihi quicquam occurrit cur, etc.,; : Atheniensium classis demersae et exercitus deleti occurrebant,; cf.: ea cum universa occurrerent animo,: oculis ejus tot paludes occurrerent,: oras ad Eurum sequentibus nihil memorabile occurrit,: animo,presents itself to his mind, occurs to him,; cf.: ea quae occurrant,: una defensio occurrit, quod muneribus tuis obniti non debui,: cogitationi, quonam modo, etc.,: neque vos paeon, aut herous ille conturbet: ipsi occurrent orationi,will present themselves,: haec tenenda sunt oratori: saepe enim occurrunt,often occur,: quodcumque in mentem veniat, aut quodcumque occurrat,: ne quid honestum occurreret,.— With inf.: occurrit et aliqua dicere de magicis (herbis),it seems proper,.—
To reach, attain (eccl. Lat.): donec occurramus in unitatem fidei,: si quo modo occurram ad resurrectionem,.

v. freq. n. [occurro], to run, go, or come to meet; to meet (not in Cic.).
Lit.
In gen.: alios occursantes interficere,: occursare capro ... caveto,beware of meeting,: fugientibus,.— Of things: occursantes inter se radices,.—
In partic.
To rush against or upon, to attack, charge; to strive against, oppose: occursat ocius gladio,: inter invidos, occursantes, factiosos,opposing,: fortissimus quisque et promptissimus ad occursandum pugnandumque,. —
To come to or towards: quid tu huc occursas,.—
Trop.
To be beforehand with, to anticipate: fortunae,.—
To appear before, present one's self to: numinibus,.—
Esp., to appear to the mind; to suggest itself, enter the thoughts, occur to one; with or without animo; also with acc. of the person: occursant animo scripta,: occursant verba,: me occursant multae, meminisse hau possum,occur to me,.

la:verb:occludo.html:
occlūdo, si, sum, 3 (
sync. form occlusti for occlusisti, .—Collat. form occlaudo, Cod. Th. 11, 24, 1), v. a.
obclaudo
, to shut or close up.
Lit. (class.): FORES OCLVDITO, Lex Puteol. ap. Haubold, p. 72: occlude ostium: et ego hinc occludam,: januam,: aedes,; : tabernas,; : furax servus, cui domi nihil sit nec obsignatum nec occlusum,: ego occlusero fontem, Att. ap. : me non excludet ab se, sed apud se occludet domi,.—
Transf., to restrain, stop: linguam, i. e. to prevent from speaking (ante-class.): occlusti linguam,; : aures,to close, shut, Oud.: os,: libidinem,to restrain,.—Hence, occlūsus (obcl-), a, um, P. a., shut or closed up.—Comp.: qui occlusiorem habeant stultiloquentiam,they would keep their foolish talk more to themselves,.—Sup.: ostium occlusissimum, (dub.; Fleck. oculissumum).

la:verb:occaeco.html:
occaeco (obc-), āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
obcaeco
,
to make blind, to blind, to deprive of sight.
Lit.
In gen. (only postAug.; cf. excaeco): quidam subito occaecati sunt,are made blind, lose their sight,: requirendum est, num oculi ejus occaecati sint,: in occaecatum pulvere effuso hostem,; .—
Transf.
To make dark; to darken, obscure: solem vides, Satin' ut occaecatus est prae hujus corporis candoribus,: densa caligo occaecaverat diem,.—Absol.: noctis et nimbūm occaecat nigror, Poët. ap. .—
To hide, conceal (so in Cic.): terra semen occaecatum cohibet,: fossas,; .—
Trop.
Of speech, to make dark, obscure, unintelligible: obscura narratio totam occaecat orationem,.—
Mentally, to make blind, to blind: stultitiā occaecatus,: occaecatus cupiditate,: nec quid agerent, ira et pavore occaecatis animis, cernebant,: consilia,: occaecatus irā,.—
To render senseless, deprive of feeling, to benumb (poet.): timor occaecaverat artus,.

la:noun:Octavius.html:
Octāvĭus, i, m.; Octāvĭa, ae, f.,
the name of a Roman gens, ; cf. Drumann, History of Rome, vol. iv. p. 218 sq.
C. Octavius, the father of theemperor Augustus, ; .—
Cn. Octavius, the first consul of this gens, .—
M. Octavius Caecina, a tribune of the people, .—
Rarely of the emperor Augustus, .—
In the fem., Octavia, the name of the two sisters of the emperor Augustus, ; ; .—
Octavia was also the name of the daughter of the emperor Claudius and Messalina, ; .—
Octaviae Porticus, two halls in Rome, ; ; ; Paul. ex Müll.—Hence,
Octāvĭānus, a, um, adj., of or belonging to an Octavius, Octavian: Octaviano bello,i. e. in the war of the consul Cn. Octavius with Cinna,: milites,of M. Octavius, who fought for Pompey,.—Esp., subst.: Octāvĭānus, i, m., a surname of the emperor Augustus, who was adopted out of the gens Octavia into the gens Julia, ; ; ; .

la:noun:occidio.html:
occīdĭo, ōnis, f.
1. occīdo
,
a massacre, utter destruction, extermination (rare before the Aug. period; syn.: clades, strages, caedes): orare ne in occidione victoriam poneret,.—Esp. freq. in the phrase occidione occidere or caedere, to cut off completely, cut down with utter destruction: equitatus occidione occisus,; ; ; ; et saep.: omnes occidione caesi,; ; so, occidione occumbere,to be wholly cut off,: equi, viri, cuncta victa occidioni dantur,every thing captured was destroyed,: occidioni exempti,fin.—Of animals and plants: nec ad occidionem gens interimenda est,: occidionem gregis prohibens,: nec ad occidionem universum genus perduci patimur,.
